metadata.narrative: Write a synthesis report on the applications of AI in drug discovery for a technical audience unfamiliar with biology. It should cover the main applications of AI in every stage of the drug discovery process, the latest technological advancements, challenges, and current adoption in the real world.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Artificial intelligence has become embedded across nearly every stage of the drug discovery pipeline, promising to compress a process that traditionally takes ten to twenty years and costs two to three billion dollars, reflecting an eighty-fold decline in R&D productivity over fifty years.

In target identification, deep learning models analyze multiomics data such as genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to compare diseased versus healthy tissue and flag genes whose activity patterns make them attractive, sometimes previously unknown, therapeutic targets.

A key complication is polypharmacology: a single drug may interact with thirty to three hundred proteins, many unknown in advance, and platforms like Cyclica's Ligand Express map this broader interaction landscape beyond one intended target.

Once a target is chosen, lead optimization relies on molecular dynamics simulations and generative adversarial networks that propose and refine candidate molecules matching desired physiochemical properties.

The most advanced generative techniques for structure-based design use diffusion models and graph neural networks, such as TargetDiff, Pocket2Mol, GraphBP, DiffSBDD, and AlphaDrug, which build three-dimensional ligands atom-by-atom inside a protein pocket and are benchmarked on docking score, drug-likeness, and synthetic accessibility.

Commercial platforms such as Iktos combine similar generative modeling with AI-driven retrosynthesis planning through its Spaya engine, claiming up to a thirty percent reduction in time and cost to reach clinical trials.

A parallel advance is Molecular Transformer, which treats chemical reactions as translation between SMILES strings using transformer attention, predicting reaction outcomes correctly over ninety percent of the time and, when trained on Pfizer's proprietary lab data, reaching ninety-seven percent accuracy with ninety-one percent retrosynthesis success.

Large language models now extend further into chemistry, editing molecular properties from natural-language prompts as in MoleculeSTM, predicting molecular properties as in Meta's Galactica, planning multi-step retrosynthesis interactively, and generating de novo molecules from text descriptions via models like MolT5.
Protein structure prediction underpins much of this work, and DeepMind's AlphaFold illustrates both the promise and the current limits of AI in this domain.

AlphaFold's initial version helped close a longstanding gap by predicting three-dimensional shapes for nearly all two hundred million known proteins, offering a faster, cheaper alternative to X-ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy, though at its debut no new drug had yet been directly attributed to its use.

AlphaFold 3, released in 2024, models interactions among proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and ions using an improved Evoformer module paired with a diffusion-based denoising process, achieving fifty percent greater accuracy on protein-ligand interactions than prior methods, though DeepMind restricted commercial drug-target predictions to protect its Isomorphic Labs spin-off.

Beyond molecule design, AI supports ADMET prediction through quantitative structure-activity relationship models estimating absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity computationally, reducing reliance on animal testing and catching liabilities like hepatotoxicity earlier.

AI also accelerates drug repurposing by mining drug-target interaction data for new indications of approved compounds, a strategy proven during COVID-19 when BenevolentAI's repurposed candidate and AbCellera's AI-discovered antibody Bamlanivimab both received FDA Emergency Use Authorization.

In clinical development, AI improves patient identification by predicting toxicity and efficacy from genomic profiles, addressing the fact that roughly eighty-six percent of trials miss enrollment deadlines; Tempus has cut trial activation time to about ten business days versus an eight-month industry average.

Digital twins, AI-generated virtual patient models simulating dosing and progression, can shrink control-group sizes by roughly thirty percent, while Roche's AI-powered digital biomarkers in its prasinezumab Phase II trial ran twice as fast with a seventy-percent leaner sample.

Real-world adoption dates to the 2012 deep-learning inflection point marked by AlexNet, after which Atomwise, Exscientia, AbCellera, and later Insilico Medicine were founded to apply neural networks to molecule design and target discovery.

Insilico Medicine reached a preclinical candidate for a known target in twenty-one days in 2019, and later achieved candidate selection for about $2.6 million and eighteen months against an industry benchmark of roughly $670 million and 4.5 years.

Exscientia's AI-designed molecule for Sumitomo Pharma, targeting obsessive-compulsive disorder, entered human trials in early 2020 after roughly twelve months of design, compared with an expected five years.
Despite this progress, no fully AI-discovered drug has yet received FDA approval, and Insilico's IPF candidate INS018_055 remains in Phase II trials rather than on the market.

The sector has weathered visible setbacks, including discontinuation of Exscientia's cancer candidate EXS21546, the Phase 3 failure of a Sumitomo/Otsuka schizophrenia candidate screened by an AI behavioral platform, and BenevolentAI's dermatitis candidate BEN-2293 failing against placebo, triggering layoffs and a steep valuation drop.

The industry is consolidating through acquisitions such as Roche's $1.9 billion purchase of Flatiron Health and Recursion's acquisitions of Cyclica and Valence Labs, alongside deepening involvement from big tech firms like NVIDIA's Clara Discovery, Microsoft's Azure-hosted language models, and Alphabet's Isomorphic Labs partnering with Eli Lilly and Novartis.

Persistent challenges include curating high-quality, unbiased training data, since public repositories often contain errors that limit convolutional neural network-based virtual screening performance.

Deep learning's "black box" nature limits interpretability, raising concerns about overfitting and poor generalization when models trained on narrow datasets face diverse real-world patient populations.

Regulatory uncertainty compounds this, as the FDA requires clear understanding of a drug's mechanism of action and substantial trial data before approval, standards complex AI-designed candidates have not yet fully satisfied.

A more alarming challenge is dual-use risk: researchers showed that a legitimate generative model called MegaSyn, built to reward bioactivity and penalize toxicity, could be inverted in under six hours to generate over 40,000 molecules including the nerve agent VX and potentially deadlier undiscovered toxins.

Taken together, AI has demonstrably accelerated early discovery timelines and unlocked new generative and structural-modeling capabilities, but validated clinical success, regulatory clarity, and safeguards against misuse remain the field's central unresolved frontiers.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
Artificial intelligence has become embedded across nearly every stage of the drug discovery pipeline, promising to compress a process that traditionally takes ten to twenty years and costs between two and three billion dollars, with roughly an eighty-fold decline in R&D productivity over the past fifty years.
[shard_06231_35603] [shard_02044_16728]

In the target identification stage, deep learning models analyze multiomics data such as genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to compare diseased versus healthy tissue and flag genes whose activity patterns make them attractive, sometimes previously unknown, therapeutic targets.
[shard_01778_82827]

A major complication at this stage is polypharmacology: a single drug may interact with anywhere from thirty to three hundred proteins in the body, many unknown in advance, and AI-driven platforms like Cyclica's Ligand Express attempt to map this broader interaction landscape beyond a single intended target.
[shard_06231_35603]

Once a target is chosen, hit discovery and lead optimization rely on molecular dynamics simulations and generative models, including generative adversarial networks, to propose and refine candidate molecules that bind the target with the desired physiochemical properties.
[shard_01778_82827]

The most advanced generative techniques for structure-based drug design use diffusion models and graph neural networks, such as TargetDiff, Pocket2Mol, GraphBP, DiffSBDD, and AlphaDrug, which build three-dimensional ligands atom-by-atom directly inside a protein pocket and are benchmarked on metrics like docking score, drug-likeness, and synthetic accessibility.
[shard_06519_8313]

Commercial platforms such as Iktos apply similar generative deep learning, combined with AI-driven retrosynthesis planning through its Spaya engine, to multi-parametric optimization of small molecules, claiming up to a thirty percent reduction in time and cost to reach clinical trials.
[shard_04365_72117]

A parallel technological advance is Molecular Transformer, which treats chemical reactions as a translation problem between SMILES strings using transformer attention mechanisms, predicting reaction outcomes correctly over ninety percent of the time and, when trained on Pfizer's proprietary lab data, reaching ninety-seven percent accuracy alongside a ninety-one percent success rate for retrosynthesis steps.
[shard_01104_83802]

Large language models are now being extended further into chemistry for tasks such as editing a molecule's properties from a natural-language prompt, as in the MoleculeSTM model, predicting molecular properties as in Meta's Galactica, planning multi-step retrosynthesis interactively, and generating de novo molecules from text descriptions via models like MolT5.
[shard_05943_40192]

Protein structure prediction underpins much of this work, and DeepMind's AlphaFold illustrates both the promise and the current limits of AI in this domain.
[shard_00200_57883]

AlphaFold's initial version helped close a longstanding gap by predicting three-dimensional shapes for nearly all two hundred million known proteins, offering a faster and cheaper alternative to X-ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy, though as of its debut no new drug had yet been directly attributed to its use.
[shard_00200_57883]

The 2024 release of AlphaFold 3 represents a substantial technological leap, modeling interactions among proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and ions using an improved Evoformer module paired with a diffusion-based denoising process, achieving fifty percent greater accuracy on protein-ligand interactions than prior methods, though DeepMind restricted commercial drug-target predictions to protect its Isomorphic Labs spin-off's business interests.
[shard_04109_57762]

Beyond molecule design, AI supports ADMET prediction through quantitative structure-activity relationship models that estimate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity computationally, reducing reliance on costly animal testing and catching liabilities like hepatotoxicity earlier.
[shard_01778_82827]

AI also accelerates drug repurposing by mining drug-target interaction datasets to find new indications for already-approved compounds, a strategy that proved valuable during the COVID-19 pandemic when BenevolentAI's repurposed candidate received FDA Emergency Use Authorization and AbCellera's AI-discovered antibody Bamlanivimab received similar authorization.
[shard_02303_44801]

In clinical development, AI improves patient identification by predicting toxicity and efficacy from genomic profiles, addresses the fact that roughly eighty-six percent of trials miss enrollment deadlines, and companies like Tempus have cut trial activation time to about ten business days versus an eight-month industry average.
[shard_05470_80992]

Digital twins, AI-generated virtual models of patients that simulate dosing and progression, can shrink control-group sizes by roughly thirty percent, while Roche's use of AI-powered digital biomarkers in its prasinezumab Phase II trial ran twice as fast with a seventy-percent leaner sample.
[shard_05470_80992] [shard_00926_73826]

Real-world industry adoption dates back to the 2012 deep-learning inflection point marked by AlexNet, after which companies including Atomwise, Exscientia, AbCellera, and later Insilico Medicine were founded to apply neural networks to small-molecule design and target discovery.
[shard_05845_27817]

Insilico Medicine reached a preclinical candidate for a known target in just twenty-one days in 2019, and by comparing its overall pipeline economics, later achieved candidate selection for about $2.6 million and eighteen months against an industry benchmark of roughly $670 million and 4.5 years.
[shard_05845_27817] [shard_02044_16728]

Exscientia's AI-designed molecule for Sumitomo Pharma, targeting obsessive-compulsive disorder, became one of the first AI-designed drugs to enter human trials in early 2020 after roughly twelve months of design, compared with an expected five years.
[shard_06450_28885] [shard_02303_44801]

Despite this progress, as of the most recent reporting, no fully AI-discovered drug has received FDA approval, and Insilico's IPF candidate INS018_055 remains in Phase II trials rather than on the market.
[shard_02151_79709]

The sector has also weathered visible setbacks, including the discontinuation of Exscientia's cancer candidate EXS21546, the Phase 3 failure of a Sumitomo/Otsuka schizophrenia candidate screened by PsychoGenics's AI behavioral platform, and BenevolentAI's atopic dermatitis candidate BEN-2293 failing to beat placebo, which triggered layoffs and a steep valuation drop.
[shard_05845_27817]

The industry is consolidating through acquisitions such as Roche's $1.9 billion purchase of Flatiron Health and Recursion Pharmaceuticals' acquisitions of Cyclica and Valence Labs, alongside deepening involvement from big technology firms like NVIDIA's Clara Discovery platform, Microsoft's Azure-hosted large language models, and Alphabet's Isomorphic Labs partnering with Eli Lilly and Novartis.
[shard_05845_27817]

Persistent challenges include curating high-quality, unbiased training data, since public repositories often contain errors that limit convolutional neural network-based virtual screening performance.
[shard_01778_82827] [shard_06231_35603]

Deep learning's "black box" nature limits interpretability, raising concerns about overfitting and poor generalization when models trained on narrow datasets are applied to diverse real-world patient populations.
[shard_05472_50470]

Regulatory uncertainty compounds this problem, as the FDA requires clear understanding of a drug's mechanism of action and substantial clinical trial data before approval, standards that complex AI-designed candidates have not yet fully satisfied.
[shard_02151_79709]

A distinct and more alarming challenge is dual-use risk: researchers demonstrated that a legitimate generative model called MegaSyn, normally built to reward bioactivity and penalize toxicity, could be inverted in under six hours to generate over 40,000 molecules including the nerve agent VX and other undiscovered, potentially deadlier toxic compounds.
[shard_00627_61902]

Taken together, AI has demonstrably accelerated early discovery timelines and unlocked new generative and structural-modeling capabilities, but validated clinical success, regulatory clarity, and safeguards against misuse remain the field's central unresolved frontiers.
[shard_05845_27817] [shard_05472_50470] [shard_00627_61902]

answer.text: Artificial intelligence has become embedded across nearly every stage of the drug discovery pipeline, promising to compress a process that traditionally takes ten to twenty years and costs two to three billion dollars, reflecting an eighty-fold decline in R&D productivity over fifty years.

In target identification, deep learning models analyze multiomics data such as genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to compare diseased versus healthy tissue and flag genes whose activity patterns make them attractive, sometimes previously unknown, therapeutic targets.

A key complication is polypharmacology: a single drug may interact with thirty to three hundred proteins, many unknown in advance, and platforms like Cyclica's Ligand Express map this broader interaction landscape beyond one intended target.

Once a target is chosen, lead optimization relies on molecular dynamics simulations and generative adversarial networks that propose and refine candidate molecules matching desired physiochemical properties.

The most advanced generative techniques for structure-based design use diffusion models and graph neural networks, such as TargetDiff, Pocket2Mol, GraphBP, DiffSBDD, and AlphaDrug, which build three-dimensional ligands atom-by-atom inside a protein pocket and are benchmarked on docking score, drug-likeness, and synthetic accessibility.

Commercial platforms such as Iktos combine similar generative modeling with AI-driven retrosynthesis planning through its Spaya engine, claiming up to a thirty percent reduction in time and cost to reach clinical trials.

A parallel advance is Molecular Transformer, which treats chemical reactions as translation between SMILES strings using transformer attention, predicting reaction outcomes correctly over ninety percent of the time and, when trained on Pfizer's proprietary lab data, reaching ninety-seven percent accuracy with ninety-one percent retrosynthesis success.

Large language models now extend further into chemistry, editing molecular properties from natural-language prompts as in MoleculeSTM, predicting molecular properties as in Meta's Galactica, planning multi-step retrosynthesis interactively, and generating de novo molecules from text descriptions via models like MolT5.
Protein structure prediction underpins much of this work, and DeepMind's AlphaFold illustrates both the promise and the current limits of AI in this domain.

AlphaFold's initial version helped close a longstanding gap by predicting three-dimensional shapes for nearly all two hundred million known proteins, offering a faster, cheaper alternative to X-ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy, though at its debut no new drug had yet been directly attributed to its use.

AlphaFold 3, released in 2024, models interactions among proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and ions using an improved Evoformer module paired with a diffusion-based denoising process, achieving fifty percent greater accuracy on protein-ligand interactions than prior methods, though DeepMind restricted commercial drug-target predictions to protect its Isomorphic Labs spin-off.

Beyond molecule design, AI supports ADMET prediction through quantitative structure-activity relationship models estimating absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity computationally, reducing reliance on animal testing and catching liabilities like hepatotoxicity earlier.

AI also accelerates drug repurposing by mining drug-target interaction data for new indications of approved compounds, a strategy proven during COVID-19 when BenevolentAI's repurposed candidate and AbCellera's AI-discovered antibody Bamlanivimab both received FDA Emergency Use Authorization.

In clinical development, AI improves patient identification by predicting toxicity and efficacy from genomic profiles, addressing the fact that roughly eighty-six percent of trials miss enrollment deadlines; Tempus has cut trial activation time to about ten business days versus an eight-month industry average.

Digital twins, AI-generated virtual patient models simulating dosing and progression, can shrink control-group sizes by roughly thirty percent, while Roche's AI-powered digital biomarkers in its prasinezumab Phase II trial ran twice as fast with a seventy-percent leaner sample.

Real-world adoption dates to the 2012 deep-learning inflection point marked by AlexNet, after which Atomwise, Exscientia, AbCellera, and later Insilico Medicine were founded to apply neural networks to molecule design and target discovery.

Insilico Medicine reached a preclinical candidate for a known target in twenty-one days in 2019, and later achieved candidate selection for about $2.6 million and eighteen months against an industry benchmark of roughly $670 million and 4.5 years.

Exscientia's AI-designed molecule for Sumitomo Pharma, targeting obsessive-compulsive disorder, entered human trials in early 2020 after roughly twelve months of design, compared with an expected five years.
Despite this progress, no fully AI-discovered drug has yet received FDA approval, and Insilico's IPF candidate INS018_055 remains in Phase II trials rather than on the market.

The sector has weathered visible setbacks, including discontinuation of Exscientia's cancer candidate EXS21546, the Phase 3 failure of a Sumitomo/Otsuka schizophrenia candidate screened by an AI behavioral platform, and BenevolentAI's dermatitis candidate BEN-2293 failing against placebo, triggering layoffs and a steep valuation drop.

The industry is consolidating through acquisitions such as Roche's $1.9 billion purchase of Flatiron Health and Recursion's acquisitions of Cyclica and Valence Labs, alongside deepening involvement from big tech firms like NVIDIA's Clara Discovery, Microsoft's Azure-hosted language models, and Alphabet's Isomorphic Labs partnering with Eli Lilly and Novartis.

Persistent challenges include curating high-quality, unbiased training data, since public repositories often contain errors that limit convolutional neural network-based virtual screening performance.

Deep learning's "black box" nature limits interpretability, raising concerns about overfitting and poor generalization when models trained on narrow datasets face diverse real-world patient populations.

Regulatory uncertainty compounds this, as the FDA requires clear understanding of a drug's mechanism of action and substantial trial data before approval, standards complex AI-designed candidates have not yet fully satisfied.

A more alarming challenge is dual-use risk: researchers showed that a legitimate generative model called MegaSyn, built to reward bioactivity and penalize toxicity, could be inverted in under six hours to generate over 40,000 molecules including the nerve agent VX and potentially deadlier undiscovered toxins.

Taken together, AI has demonstrably accelerated early discovery timelines and unlocked new generative and structural-modeling capabilities, but validated clinical success, regulatory clarity, and safeguards against misuse remain the field's central unresolved frontiers.
